exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with rheumatic fever presents with dyspnoea; ECG shows P‑wave 130 ms. What is the most likely diagnosis and next investigation? — Recognise LAE; order chest X‑ray or bedside echo to assess mitral valve.
You find a double‑density sign on X‑ray in a hypertensive patient. How does this change your management? — Identify LAE; tighten blood pressure control and screen for AF.

A patient with known LAE develops an irregular pulse. What is the immediate priority? — Confirm atrial fibrillation, assess haemodynamic stability, and start rate control plus anticoagulation if stable.
Why is warfarin preferred over direct oral anticoagulants in many low‑resource settings for LAE‑related AF? — Warfarin is cheaper, monitoring INR is feasible; DOACs may be unavailable or costly.
Explain how anemia from malaria can exacerbate left atrial enlargement. — Chronic anemia raises cardiac output, increasing volume load on the left atrium.
A trainee orders a CT scan to measure left atrial size. What is a more appropriate test in this setting? — Hand‑held cardiac ultrasound or ECG/X‑ray; CT is rarely available and unnecessary.
What are red‑flag signs that indicate urgent referral for a patient with LAE? — Pulmonary oedema, rapid AF with hypotension, or signs of valve rupture.
Differentiate P‑mitrale from right atrial enlargement on ECG. — P‑mitrale: broad, notched P in II; right atrial enlargement: tall peaked P in II, often with right axis deviation.
ai.title: Left Atrial Enlargement
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Left atrial enlargement (LAE) reflects chronic pressure or volume overload of the left atrium. It is common in rheumatic heart disease, hypertension, and mitral valve disease in low‑resource settings. Recognising LAE guides management and predicts complications such as atrial fibrillation and stroke.

b: Pressure overload – e.g., mitral stenosis, systemic hypertension
Volume overload – e.g., mitral regurgitation, atrial septal defect
sections.p: The left atrium receives pulmonary venous return and transfers blood to the left ventricle. Chronic overload stretches the atrial wall, increasing its size on imaging or ECG.

b: ECG: P‑wave >120 ms in lead II (P mitrale) or biphasic P in V1
Chest X‑ray: double‑density sign on the right side of the cardiac silhouette
sections.p: LAE is diagnosed by ECG criteria, chest X‑ray, or echocardiography. In low‑resource hospitals, ECG and plain X‑ray are often the only available tools.

b: Atrial fibrillation → risk of stroke, especially with HIV‑related hypercoagulability
Progressive dyspnoea from left‑sided heart failure
sections.p: LAE predisposes to atrial fibrillation, thrombo‑embolism, and heart failure. In East Africa, rheumatic mitral stenosis remains a leading cause.

t.b: Does the patient have electrical evidence of LAE? → P‑wave >120 ms or biphasic P in V1 suggests enlargement.
Is there radiographic enlargement of the left atrium? → Double‑density sign confirms LAE.
What is the atrial size and valve function? → LA diameter >40 mm (parasternal long axis) confirms LAE and identifies mitral pathology.

b: Control hypertension with thiazide diuretics or ACE inhibitors (avoid ACE‑inhibitor cough in patients with active TB).
Repair or replace rheumatic mitral valve when feasible; otherwise use beta‑blockers for rate control.
Anticoagulation with warfarin for persistent AF and LAE (monitor INR; if INR testing unavailable, use clinical risk scoring and consider low‑dose aspirin only if bleeding risk is high).
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control rate/rhythm if atrial fibrillation occurs, and prevent thrombo‑embolism.

b: Ignoring the contribution of anemia or high output states to volume overload.
Starting anticoagulation without confirming atrial fibrillation in a patient with bleeding risk.
sections.p: Misinterpreting a tall P‑wave as isolated atrial enlargement without considering mitral disease, or assuming normal X‑ray rules out LAE.

b: Link P‑wave changes to specific valve lesions.
Prioritise treatment of the underlying cause before anticoagulation.
sections.p: Examiners often test integration of ECG, imaging, and management decisions.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe dyspnoea or pulmonary oedema
New rapid irregular pulse suggesting atrial fibrillation
Chest pain with hypotension indicating possible mitral valve rupture
